"Start your usual sport in one tap"

"Energy starts after your first night. Sleep is what fills it."
"Not shown while taking beta-blockers or during pregnancy: resting heart rate doesn't reflect fitness then."
"Put the strap on its charger, close to this phone."
"Recovery is scored each morning from the night's sleep."
"The server address must start with https://"
"Without location, distance comes from the strap's steps."
"Health Connect isn't available on this phone."
"Keeping it at %1$s or more week after week is what counts."
"Under %1$s every day in the last 30, between %2$s and %3$s."
"At %1$s or more every day with a total in the last 30."
"At %1$s or more on %2$s of %3$s days in the last 30."
"Your usual shows after a week of wear."
"%1$s, as hard as or harder than %2$s%% of your days in the last 3 months."
"%1$s, easier than %2$s%% of your days in the last 3 months."
"Your last 7 days are well above your usual, so you're building."
"Your last 7 days are well below your usual, so you're easing off."
"Your last 7 days are close to your usual, a steady stretch."
"From your latest workout the strap could read it from."
"Estimated from your profile and resting heart rate, updated weekly."
"Your body uses about %1$s kcal a day at rest, before any movement."
"Found a strap nearby. Pick it to pair."
"Connecting to your strap. Keep it close."
"Couldn't connect yet. Keep the strap on its charger, near the phone."
"The strap turned the key down. Open your strap to pair again."
"The strap recorded %1$s of the %2$s so far today."
"The strap was worn for part of the day, so its totals are low."
"Steps, calories and Energy count only the time the strap was on. Charging pauses them too."
"When the strap was worn for under %1$s of the day, or under that share of the day so far."
"Over the last 12 months, weeks averaged from %1$s to %2$s%3$s."
"One score in the last 7 days so far."
"Averaged %1$s over the last 7 days, from %2$s to %3$s."
"Started the day at %1$s and ended it at %2$s."
"Your normal shows after %1$s %2$s with data. %3$s so far."
"You are here. Your normal is %1$s to %2$s%3$s, from %4$s %5$s."
"How fast your heart beats, in beats per minute (bpm), read by the strap through the day and night."

"The strap reads your pulse with light through the skin, about once a minute, and more often in a workout or while Live is on. The band behind the day's line is your resting range: your usual resting heart rate, give or take a usual spread, over the last 30 days."
"Movement, stress, caffeine and heat raise it. Rest and sleep bring it down."
"A loose strap, cold hands or busy arm movement can make readings jump. Live readings come more often, so the line looks busier while it's on."
"Your heart rate at its calmest. Lower usually means a fitter, well rested heart."
"The strap works it out each day from your calmest stretch, usually in sleep. Your normal is the middle of your last 30 days, give or take a usual spread, once 7 of them have a value."
"It rises after hard training, late meals, alcohol, poor sleep or when your body is fighting something off, and falls as fitness builds."
"A night with the strap loose or off gives it less to go on. One high day says less than a few in a row."
"Heart rate variability, the small changes in time between heartbeats. Higher than your usual means your body has recovered."

"The strap measures the time between beats, in milliseconds (ms), while you're still, mostly in sleep, and the day's value is the average of its readings. It's read against your own normal: the middle of your last 30 days, give or take a usual spread."
"Good sleep and rest raise it. Stress, hard training and alcohol lower it. Compare it with your own normal, not other people's."
"Moving during a reading, a loose strap or a short night leave fewer clean readings. HRV swings a lot from day to day, so a few days in a row say more than one."
"How much of your blood's capacity is carrying oxygen. Most people sit at 95 to 100%%."
"The strap shines red and infrared light through the skin and compares how much of each comes back. The day's value is the average of its readings."
"Altitude and pauses in breathing during sleep can lower it."
"A loose strap, cold skin or moving during a reading can give low values. It's a wellness reading, not a medical one."
"The strap's stress level from 0 to 100. Higher means your body is more on alert."
"The strap works it out from your heart rate and its variability while you're still. Readings during and just after a workout are left out, since exercise isn't stress."
"Pressure, caffeine and too little sleep raise it. Calm breathing, rest and time outdoors bring it down."
"Excitement, heat and an illness look like stress to the strap. Small movements while sitting can push it up."
"The temperature of your skin under the strap. What matters is the change from your normal, not the level."
"The strap measures it against your skin. The level depends on fit and the room, so OpenStrap shows it as a change from your normal of the last 30 days."
"It moves with alcohol, a warm room, hard training, the menstrual cycle, or when your body is fighting something off."
"A warm bed, a heavy duvet or the strap sitting loose all change it without your body changing."
"How many breaths you take a minute while asleep. It stays very steady for most people."
"The strap measures it during sleep, so there's one value a night, read against your normal of the last 30 days."
"It can rise above your normal after a hard training day, in a warm, stuffy room, or when your body is fighting something off."
"A restless night, or the strap off for part of it, leaves fewer readings to go on."
"Steps counted by the strap through the day."
"The strap counts them from your arm's movement and keeps them minute by minute. A day's steps are the total of its minutes."
"Short walks spread across the day add up. Most people aim for 7,000 to 10,000."
"Pushing a pram or a trolley, or holding a rail, hides steps. Waving your arms about can add a few."
"How ready your body is for effort today, from 0 to 100, worked out each morning from your night."

"Each morning OpenStrap compares your night with what's normal for you, not with other people: HRV (heart rate variability), resting heart rate, skin temperature, breathing rate and blood oxygen, last night's sleep and the past few nights, and how hard yesterday was. About half the score comes from HRV and resting heart rate, about a quarter from sleep. One signal far from your normal caps it, so good sleep can't fully make up for it. Everything is worked out on this phone from your strap's data."
"Good sleep, easy days and nights without alcohol lift it. Hard training, short nights, late meals, stress and illness hold it down."
"It needs %1$s good nights to start and settles over %2$s. A night with the strap loose or off, or too few clean HRV readings, gives it less to go on, and the strap's own readings may stand in."
"Your energy right now, from 0 to 100. Sleep fills it and the day uses it."

"Think of it as a battery that runs all day. Sleep fills it, deep sleep most of all, and a calm, steady night fills it faster. Being awake uses a little every hour. Exercise and stress use it faster, while quiet, relaxed moments slow the drain. It's worked out on this phone from your heart rate, minute by minute, as a guide to plan your day, not medical advice."
"A long, calm night fills it more. Workouts, a stressful day and a late night use it up."
"Energy starts after your first night. With the strap off overnight there's no sleep to fill it from, so the day starts from your usual Energy at waking, an estimate."
"How well you slept, from 0 to 100, scored by the strap from the night."

"The score is the strap's own, from the length and the stages of the night, and it mostly follows how long you slept. The stages are light, deep and REM (rapid eye movement), when most dreams happen. What shaped the score rates the night against general sleep guidance: time asleep against your sleep need, and staying asleep, with under 30 minutes awake after falling asleep counting as settled. Too much sleep counts against it too, past 9½ hours. Stages aren't rated, since a strap reads them less surely than sleep from waking. It's a guide, not a medical assessment."
"Regular bedtimes, a dark, cool room and less caffeine and alcohol late in the day help. Late nights, a restless night and waking early pull it down."
"Lying still awake can count as asleep, and light and deep sleep are hard to tell apart through the skin. A night with the strap off or loose may be missed or cut short."
"How alike your sleep and wake times are from one day to the next. 100 is the same every day."

"OpenStrap works out the Sleep Regularity Index. It marks each minute of the day asleep or awake and counts how often a minute matches the same minute the day before, over the last 7 days. It needs %1$s h of wear compared day to day, about 5 days worn around the clock, and until then shows how much the middle of your sleep moved. The bands follow how UK Biobank adults scored, where half of them were between 74 and 86. Your usual times are the average of the last 7 nights."
"Going to bed and getting up at the same times, weekends too, raises it. Late nights, lie-ins and long naps lower it."
"Minutes with the strap off aren't compared, so a week with little wear rests on fewer days. Lying awake in bed can count as asleep."
"Sleep in the day, which the strap records apart from your night."

"The strap tells a nap from your night itself, and records its stages when it's long enough. A nap belongs to the day it started on. Its heart rate comes from the day's readings, since the strap sends no average for a nap."
"A short nap early in the afternoon refreshes without taking much from the night. A long or late one can make it harder to fall asleep."
"Lying still awake can look like a short nap, and a short nap may have no stages."
"Points for the minutes your heart rate is raised, harder minutes earning more, over the last 7 days. Aim for %1$s."

"Heart points are the strap's PAI, Personal Activity Intelligence. The strap works them out itself from how far your heart rate rises above resting, against your age and sex, and OpenStrap shows them as they come. Each day's points count for 7 days, then drop off, so the total always covers the last week."
"Anything that gets you out of breath adds the most. Brisk walking adds a little. A few hard sessions a week keep the total at %1$s or more."
"The total updates when the strap syncs, so it can lag behind today's effort. A loose strap in a workout misses raised heart rate."
"Minutes of brisk movement or harder over the last 7 days, against the %1$s a week health guidelines aim for."

"A minute at %1$s steps or more counts as moderate, and %2$s or more as vigorous, inside a run of at least %3$s such minutes. Effort without steps, like cycling or rowing, counts from heart rate after %4$s minutes in a row at %5$s%% of your heart rate reserve or more, vigorous from %6$s%%. A vigorous minute counts double, as in the World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines."
"Brisk walks of a few minutes or more, cycling, running and sport all count. Strolling and short bursts don't."
"No study has checked a strap's step counts against walking pace, so brisk minutes near the line can be missed or counted. Pushing a trolley or holding a rail hides steps."
"How hard your heart worked today, from workouts and moving about, against your usual day."

"Each minute counts by how hard your heart works between resting and maximum, Banister's training impulse (TRIMP). Every workout minute counts. Outside workouts only moving minutes do, at 35%% of your heart rate reserve or more, or brisk walking from 20%%. Your usual is your fitness, a 42-day average of your daily Load. Building, Steady and Easing off compare the last 7 days with it, Steady within a quarter either side. Strain puts the day on a fixed curve from 0 to 21, where an hour at 60%% of your reserve is about 7."
"Workouts add the most, longer and harder ones more. A day of walking about adds a little. Rest days bring the week's balance down."

"Days the strap was mostly off are left out of your usual. A low maximum heart rate makes every minute count for more. Workouts also carry the strap's EPOC, its measure of what one workout took, on a different scale from Load."
"The most oxygen your body can use in hard effort, a measure of fitness. Higher is fitter."

"It's measured in millilitres of oxygen per kilogram of body weight a minute (ml/kg/min). After a workout the strap can read it from, the number is the strap's own estimate from your heart rate and pace. Otherwise OpenStrap estimates it from your age, sex, body mass index, resting heart rate while asleep and how active you say you are (Jurca and others, 2005), updated weekly, and shows it as a range. Where you sit for your age and sex comes from treadmill tests of thousands of adults (FRIEND, 2022)."
"Regular hard effort raises it over weeks. Weight, age and long breaks from training lower it."
"The estimate from your profile is typically within about 5 either way. A resting heart rate thrown by a short night or illness moves it."
"How long your body needs after your last workout before it's ready for another hard one."

"It's the strap's estimate, or OpenStrap's own for a workout recorded on the phone, from how hard the workout was: its EPOC, the extra oxygen your body uses afterwards to recover. The same EPOC gives each workout its training effect, from 0 to 5, for how much it builds your fitness."
"Longer and harder workouts need more time. Easy sessions need little."
"It knows only the workout, not your sleep, stress or the rest of the day. Recovery here is time, not the morning's Recovery score."
"The energy your body uses in a day, at rest and moving, in kilocalories (kcal). An estimate."

"Your body's use at rest comes from your weight, height, age and sex (Mifflin-St Jeor). On top of it come your steps each minute and, for effort without steps, your heart rate. A recorded workout uses its own kcal. Sleep counts at a little under resting."
"Moving more raises it, most of all workouts. A heavier body uses more at rest and in motion."
"Food digestion isn't included. It only covers the minutes the strap was worn, so a day with it off for hours reads low. A profile out of date throws the resting part."
"How far you walked and ran today, estimated from your steps."
"Each minute's steps times a step length from your height: %1$s%% of it at a walk, rising to %2$s%% at 130 steps a minute and faster. Without a height the strap's own figure stands in."
"More steps, and faster ones, which are longer."
"Step length varies from person to person and with hills, so it can be off by a tenth or more. A workout with GPS has its own distance."
"%1$s of %2$s minutes came from heart rate."
"Today it's read between %1$s bpm resting and %2$s bpm maximum"
"Your last 7 days against the last 4 weeks come to %1$.2f, the acute to chronic ratio. It's shown for "
"interest only, since the evidence for a safe ratio is disputed, and never enters Recovery."
"This week's estimate uses a resting heart rate of %1$s bpm, while asleep."
"That's typical of a %1$s aged about %2$s to %3$s."
"It covers %1$s of wear, so it's part of the day."
"That's an unusual total for a full day. Check your profile and how the strap was worn."
"%1$s minutes came from heart rate rather than steps."
"Opened from the night, it shows only your sleep: the line from falling asleep to waking, the lowest while asleep and the strap's average for the night. Month and Year are whole days."
"Opened from the night, it shows the strap's readings in sleep, kept apart from the spot readings in the day, against your earlier nights."
"Opened from the night, it's that night's readings, against your earlier nights."
"Opened from the night, it's the average of the readings taken while you slept, against your earlier nights. Month and Year are whole days, day and night."
"Dips in blood oxygen while you sleep, counted by the strap, as how many an hour. An early estimate."

"The strap counts each short drop in blood oxygen during sleep, and that's divided by the hours asleep. Your usual is the middle of your earlier nights, once there are %1$s of them. They are fairly steady for each person, so they're shown with your sleep rather than in Recovery."
"Alcohol, a blocked nose, sleeping on your back and altitude can raise it."
"The strap's units aren't confirmed on a real strap yet, so treat the number as an early estimate. A loose strap can read as a dip. %1$s It isn't a test for sleep apnea."
"How old your habits make your body look, as a range of years, worked out each Sunday."

"Each habit is scored against the typical person your age and sex: resting heart rate, steps, sleep regularity, time asleep, strength training and fitness (VO2 max, the most oxygen your body can use in hard effort). Better than typical takes years off, worse adds them. The total is shrunk, because the habits overlap, and capped at 5 years either way. It looks back 6 months, 3 for fitness."

"Your habits over months, not a single day. The pace of aging compares your last 30 days with those 6 months: faster than 1x means the estimate is heading up, slower means it's coming down. The Habit Age page shows what each habit takes off or adds."

"It updates once a week and is withheld until there's enough data. An estimate from under 6 months of data is early, so its range is wider. It's an estimate for personal insight, not a medical measurement, shown as a range because each habit's effect is uncertain."
"Last Monday to Sunday, day by day: how much you moved, trained and slept."

"Steps are each day's total from the strap's minutes, and steps a day the average of the days with any. Active minutes are worked out as in their own sheet. A night belongs to the evening it started, so Sunday's is the night into Monday."
"Every walk, workout and early night shows here a week later."
"Steps and workouts are compared with the week before. Active minutes and sleep only go back two weeks, so they're shown without a comparison. A day with the strap off reads low."
"Not enough wear for the full measure yet: %1$s h of the %2$s h it needs."
"Meanwhile the middle of your sleep moved about %1$s this week."
"Your sleep need here is %1$s, from your age or your own setting."
"The strap's own score today is %1$s. It doesn't count sleep length, so after a short night it reads higher than OpenStrap's. It's kept for comparison and never enters OpenStrap's score."
"Today one body signal is far from your normal, so the score is capped."
"Last night's own HRV wasn't clean enough, so the strap's %1$s ms stands in."
"Last night's own resting heart rate wasn't clean enough, so the strap's %1$s bpm stands in."
"The week's HRV rests on %1$s of 7 nights, so it's less sure than usual."
"The strap was off overnight, so today started from an estimate."
"Stress counts from %1$s: %2$s above your calm level of %3$s over the last %4$s days."
"Stress counts from %1$s for now. After %2$s of wear it adjusts to your own calm level."
"Stress counts from %1$s for now, until there are enough calm readings to find your own level."
"Lowest %1$s bpm at %2$s %3$s, %4$s on average while asleep."
"One night with an average heart rate in the last 7 so far."
"Averaged %1$s bpm asleep over the last 7 nights, from %2$s to %3$s."
"Very regular this week. Your days kept nearly the same sleep times."
"Regular this week. Most days kept similar sleep times."
"Fair this week. Your sleep times moved on some days."
"Irregular this week. Your sleep times moved a lot from day to day."
"The middle of your sleep moved about %1$s this week. The full measure needs more wear."
"Regularity needs about 5 days of wear around the clock."
"%1$s you fell asleep at %2$s and woke at %3$s"
"The strap didn't record stages for this nap."
"Last night is still on the strap."
"Keep it near your phone and it comes across."
"Your data since %1$s is still on the strap."
"Your data is still on the strap."
"Recovery shows once last night is in."
"No sleep recorded last night, so there's no score today."
"Energy shows once the strap has a few hours of heart rate."
"Your first night with the strap shows here in the morning."
"Estimated kcal, part of the day worn"
"Some overnight signals are off your normal. An easy day suits."
"Well recovered. A good day for a hard session."
"Not fully recovered. Keep the effort moderate."
"Still catching up. An easy day helps."
"OpenStrap is still learning your nights, %1$s of %2$s."
"Not enough heart data last night for a Recovery score."
"Recovery starts after your first night with the strap."
"No sleep recorded last night. Was the strap on?"
"Heart rate since the end shows once the strap sends it."
"Week on week comparisons start next Monday."
"Hold to scrub, the number follows. The band is your resting range."
"%1$s, as many as the week before."
"No Heart points from the strap for these days yet."
"No Heart points in the last 30 days yet."
"Needs the strap's steps and heart rate"
"No Load in the last %1$s days yet."
"You are here. Your usual is %1$s a day."
"Pin up to two cards under the top card, or hide the ones you don't need."
"Add age, weight and height to see it"
"No VO2 max from workouts yet, counted as typical"
"Not enough data yet, counted as typical"
", most people your age do none"
"%1$s h %2$s m, counts only below 6 h 30 m"
"Add your %1$s in your profile to see your Habit Age."
"Starts at your age. Wear the strap for 30 days for a first estimate."
"Needs 30 days with enough data, and 3 months before them to tell a real change from day-to-day noise."
"Your last 30 days beat your 6-month habits. Kept up, the estimate will come down."
"Your last 30 days fall behind your 6-month habits. Kept up, the estimate will go up."
"Your last 30 days match your 6-month habits, so the estimate is moving in step with the calendar."
"Fitness terms capped: resting heart rate, steps and VO2 max together count for at most 3 years either way."
"What drove Recovery shows here each morning"
"No sleep recorded in the last 7 nights"
"Strap off overnight, so today started from an estimate."
"%1$s %2$s–%3$s, mostly zone %4$s, %5$s bpm on average. Nobody pressed Start."
"Your heart rate has been up since %1$s, %2$s bpm on average. Record a %3$s from %4$s?"
"The strap hasn't sent heart rate for this day yet. Sync, then try again."
"Drag the handles to where the workout began and ended. Its heart rate comes from the strap's minute records."
"Rest. The strap buzzes when it's over."
"Or sooner, once heart rate drops below"
"Target. The strap buzzes if you drift out."
"After 8 min near resting heart rate and no steps, the strap buzzes and asks."
"The strap isn't connected. Recording carries on, and the minutes missed are filled from its own history after it syncs."
"Target %1$s, the strap buzzes if you drift"
"All %1$s sets done. Hold the square to end, or keep going."
"You last moved at %1$s. End the %2$s there, so the drive isn't counted?"
"Your heart rate has been back near resting since %1$s. End the %2$s at %3$s?"
"Its heart rate and times are removed from OpenStrap. The strap's own history is kept."
"Ended at %1$s. %2$s of driving were left out."
"Ended at %1$s, when you'd stopped. %2$s after that were left out."
"Trimmed to start at %1$s. The rest is kept."
"Drag the handles to where the workout really started and ended. Nothing recorded is deleted."
"Its heart rate and times are removed from OpenStrap, and the next sync won't bring it back. The strap's own history is kept."
"The strap hasn't sent this workout's heart rate yet."
"Workouts you start in OpenStrap show up here, and the strap's own after a sync."
"Not enough heart rate to work out Load."
"No Recovery in the last 7 days yet."
"Needs a few hours of heart rate"
"No sleep scores in the last 7 nights yet."
"No sleep recorded in the last 7 nights."
"%1$s asleep, no score from the strap"
"End the workout? Tap Yes, end to save it."
"How far your heart rate falls in the first minute after you stop. A bigger drop usually means a fitter heart, and under 12 bpm is on the low side. It only says something after a hard effort."
"No heart rate after the end, so no drop this time."
"Off. Distance from the strap's steps, roughly."
"Turn it on for distance and the map, or start without it."
"On. Saved on this phone for the map."
"Heart rate comes from the strap every second. GPS is on for outdoor workouts, and you can turn it off."

"The strap sends heart rate every second, with the phone's screen off too. If it drops out or isn't connected at the start, recording carries on, and the missing minutes are filled from the strap's own history after the next sync."

"Outdoors, GPS uses the phone's location during this workout only, for distance, pace and the map. Its switch turns it off for this workout. Map tiles come from OpenFreeMap, which sees roughly where the map is. Route only on the map loads no tiles. Without GPS, walks and runs get a distance from the strap's steps, marked ≈."
"With Keep the route on, the route is saved on this phone for the map. Off, only the totals are kept and the route is discarded when the workout ends."
"Heart rate drop %1$s bpm in the first minute"

"Load on a workout is EPOC: the extra oxygen your body uses afterwards to recover, in ml per kg of body weight. The harder and longer the workout, the higher it goes. It isn't the day's Load, which counts every minute on another scale. This workout: %1$s.%2$s"

"Two scales from 0 to 5. Aerobic is what the workout did for your endurance, anaerobic for short, hard efforts. Under 2 trains little, 2 to 3 keeps what you have, 3 to 4 builds on it, 4 to 5 builds a lot, and 5 is more than your body can use right away. This workout: "
"How long until your body is ready for another hard workout, from the training effect and how tired you've been lately. This workout: %1$s."
"This workout: down %1$s in the first minute"
"You finished at %1$s bpm, close to resting, so there was little to come down from and it isn't rated."
"How far your heart rate falls in the first minute after you stop. A bigger drop usually means a fitter heart, and under 12 bpm is on the low side. It only says something after a hard effort. %1$s"
"The most oxygen your body can use, in ml per kg per minute, estimated from this workout: %1$s."
"Worked out by OpenStrap from your heart rate, on the strap's own scales."
"From the strap, worked out during the workout."
" The strap recorded this workout too. Its own figures: %1$s."
"What this workout asked of your body, and what it trained."
"You are here. Aerobic %1$s on the 0 to 5 scale."
"Charging. Wear data pauses until it's back on."
"The strap keeps recording on its own, but OpenStrap won't sync or show live heart rate until you connect again."
"The strap restarts and disconnects. OpenStrap reconnects on its own once it's back, which can take a minute."

"OpenStrap will disconnect and delete the strap's address and auth key from this phone. Your synced health data stays. To pair again you'll need the auth key.\n\nThis doesn't unbind the strap from your Zepp account."
"Not linked. You can turn off battery optimization for OpenStrap instead."
"Couldn't open battery settings on this phone."
"OpenStrap keeps retrying. Keep the strap on its charger near the phone, and make sure the Zepp app isn't running. The strap talks to one app at a time."
"OpenStrap needs the strap's auth key, which Zepp creates when you link the strap. You only do this once."
"Link the strap in the Zepp app"
"Install Zepp, sign in, and link your Helio Strap."
"OpenStrap signs in with email only. If you signed up with Google or Apple, add an email and password to your account in the Zepp app's account settings."
"Force-stop or uninstall Zepp so it lets go of the strap. Don't unlink the strap in Zepp: that wipes its key."
"Sign in with the same Zepp email. OpenStrap finds your strap and its key, then pairs."
"Scan with the strap on its charger and tap it to fill in the address, then paste the 32-character auth key. The dBm beside each strap is its signal, and nearer zero is closer."
"Scanning stopped: %1$s. Check that Bluetooth is on and try again."
"Looking for straps nearby. Keep the strap on its charger."
"The auth key must be 32 characters of 0–9 and a–f. You entered %1$s."
"The Bluetooth address should look like C8:0F:10:AB:CD:EF. Scan to fill it in."
"Zepp sign-in saved, but no auth key came with it. Get the key on a computer and enter it by hand."
"Restarting the strap. OpenStrap reconnects when it's back."
"Restored %1$,d records from before the strap's history. Left out %2$,d from days it has."
"Health Connect has no OpenStrap data to restore."
"What you aim for each day. Change them whenever they stop fitting."
"An active hour is one with at least 250 steps."
"Add age and sex for accurate effort and recovery"
"Age sets your maximum heart rate, which every effort and recovery number depends on. All fields are optional and stay on this phone."
"Sex, for energy, Load, fitness and Habit Age"
"Pick the level that best matches a usual week."
"Sleep need (7–9, blank for your age's default)"
"A zip of every synced record, saved where you choose"
"Copy your data to Android Health Connect"
"This removes every alarm from the strap."
"The strap vibrates at the alarm time. To stop it, tap the front of the strap several times."
"Heart rate alerts need continuous or every-minute measuring."
"The strap vibrates when an alert goes off. OpenStrap isn't a medical device."
"The strap buzzes while your phone rings, and for calls from apps like WhatsApp with notification access. With Do Not Disturb on, only if it allows calls from anyone."
"The strap buzzes for notifications that would make a sound."
